descricao: Four productive suffixes that turn one word into many: -ous (noun → adjective), -able/-ible (verb → adjective), -tion/-ment/-ness (verb/adjective → noun), and -er/-or/-ist (verb/field → person). Learn to read any unknown word by recognizing its parts.

secoes.conteudo:
In English, most words belong to a family. The noun **danger** has an adjective: **dangerous**. The verb **improve** has a noun: **improvement**. The adjective **happy** has a noun: **happiness**, an adverb: **happily**, and a negative form: **unhappy**. When you learn the full family of a word rather than just one form of it, your vocabulary expands much faster — because each new root gives you not one word but four or five.

This material teaches the most productive English suffixes: the ones that build thousands of common words and follow patterns clear enough to be learned as a system. You will see how nouns become adjectives (**-ous**), how verbs become adjectives (**-able/-ible**), how verbs and adjectives become nouns (**-tion, -ment, -ness**), and how verbs and fields become person-words (**-er, -or, -ist**).

By the end, you will be able to look at an unknown English word and use its suffix to make a reliable first guess at both its meaning and its grammatical role — without opening a dictionary. That skill is called morphological awareness, and it is one of the clearest markers of a confident B1-B2 reader.

The suffix **-ous** turns nouns into adjectives meaning 'having the quality of' or 'characterized by.' Add it to a noun and you describe something that possesses that quality.

**fame** → **famous** — widely known and recognized everywhere. **danger** → **dangerous** — involving risk or the possibility of harm. **nerve** → **nervous** — full of anxiety, unable to relax. **courage** → **courageous** — willing to act despite fear. **ambition** → **ambitious** — driven by a strong desire to achieve. **luxury** → **luxurious** — characterized by great comfort and expense. **fury** → **furious** — extremely angry. **mystery** → **mysterious** — difficult to understand or explain. **glory** → **glorious** — magnificent, wonderful, brilliant.

Spelling changes: when the noun ends in a silent **-e**, it drops before **-ous** (fame → famous, nerve → nervous). When it ends in **-y**, the y changes to **i** (fury → furious, glory → glorious). When it ends in **-ge** or **-ce**, the **-e** is kept to preserve the soft sound (courage → courageous, outrage → outrageous).

Excellent news for Portuguese speakers: **-ous** words are almost always direct cognates of Portuguese **-oso** words. **Famoso** / **famous**. **Nervoso** / **nervous**. **Generoso** / **generous**. **Curioso** / **curious**. **Misterioso** / **mysterious**. **Glorioso** / **glorious**. **Furioso** / **furious**. The root is the same, the suffix is structurally identical, and the meaning is identical. If you know the Portuguese word, you almost certainly already know the English one — you just need to recognize the pattern. The main difference: in English, **-ous** is always unstressed and sounds like '-us' (rhymes with 'bus'), never '-oso.'

Both suffixes create adjectives meaning 'able to be done' or 'having this quality.' They typically attach to verbs: **comfort** → **comfortable** (can be sat in comfortably), **believe** → **believable** (can be believed), **rely** → **reliable** (can be relied upon). They also attach to nouns and Latin roots: **sense** → **sensible** (makes sense), **terror** → **terrible** (originally 'causing terror' — now simply 'very bad').

Common **-able** words: **comfortable**, **believable**, **reliable**, **affordable**, **acceptable**, **remarkable**, **reasonable**, **avoidable**, **valuable**, **considerable**, **understandable**. Common **-ible** words: **sensible**, **responsible**, **terrible**, **horrible**, **flexible**, **accessible**, **possible**, **visible**, **reversible**.

The honest grammar point: **there is no reliable rule for when to use -able versus -ible**. Broadly, **-able** appears in newer words and in words derived from full English verbs (avoid → avoidable, remark → remarkable). **-ible** appears in older, Latin-rooted words. In practice, you learn the most common ones individually and check the rest. What you can count on: if you are forming a new adjective from a verb you already know, **-able** is always the safe default. 'That is simply unthinkable.' 'The results are unbelievable.' 'The damage is unspeakable.' All newly formed words in English use **-able**.

One important negative pattern: both suffixes combine naturally with **un-**, **in-**, and **ir-** from the previous material. **Unavoidable** (un- + avoidable). **Invisible** (in- + visible). **Irresponsible** (ir- + responsible). **Impossible** (im- + possible). Seeing these longer words stops being intimidating the moment you can break them into their parts.

These three suffixes turn verbs and adjectives into nouns. They cover three different semantic categories: processes and their results (**-tion**), the products or outcomes of actions (**-ment**), and abstract qualities (**-ness**).

**-tion / -sion** is the most common noun-forming suffix in English. It turns verbs into nouns for processes, results, or states. **inform** → **information**. **create** → **creation**. **decide** → **decision**. **communicate** → **communication**. **organize** → **organization**. **educate** → **education**. **produce** → **production**. **discuss** → **discussion**. **connect** → **connection**. **permit** → **permission**. Whether a word ends in -tion or -sion depends on the verb's Latin root and has no simple rule — but the pronunciation is always identical: 'shun.' **Information** is pronounced 'in-for-MAY-shun,' **decision** is 'de-SI-zhun.' The suffix is always unstressed.

**-ment** turns verbs into nouns for the result or ongoing state of an action. **improve** → **improvement** — what you have after improving. **achieve** → **achievement** — what you have accomplished. **agree** → **agreement** — what is produced when people agree. **manage** → **management**. **develop** → **development**. **retire** → **retirement**. **disappoint** → **disappointment**. **encourage** → **encouragement**. Notice the pattern: -ment nouns often describe something that exists as a result of the verb's action — an object, a state, or a product that persists after the action.

**-ness** turns adjectives into nouns for abstract qualities — the state or condition of being that adjective. **happy** → **happiness**. **dark** → **darkness**. **kind** → **kindness**. **aware** → **awareness**. **fit** → **fitness**. **sad** → **sadness**. **lonely** → **loneliness**. **weak** → **weakness**. **ill** → **illness**. When the adjective ends in **-y**, it changes to **i** before **-ness**: happy → happiness, lonely → loneliness, ready → readiness. **-ness** is one of the most productive suffixes in English — almost any adjective can take it, and the meaning is always the same: the quality or state of being that adjective.

Three suffixes do the same job: they turn a verb or a field of knowledge into a noun for the person who practices it. The difference between them is mostly historical — which Latin or Germanic root the word came from — rather than meaningful.

**-er** is the most common suffix and attaches directly to verbs: **teach** → **teacher**, **manage** → **manager**, **write** → **writer**, **design** → **designer**, **bake** → **baker**, **lead** → **leader**, **work** → **worker**, **build** → **builder**, **read** → **reader**. Spelling note: when the verb ends in a single vowel followed by a single consonant, the consonant doubles: **run** → **runner**, **swim** → **swimmer**, **plan** → **planner**. When the verb ends in **-e**, just add **-r**: **bake** → **baker**, **write** → **writer**, **drive** → **driver**.

**-or** appears mainly in Latin-rooted words and cannot simply be swapped for -er: **act** → **actor**, **instruct** → **instructor**, **direct** → **director**, **invest** → **investor**, **visit** → **visitor**, **edit** → **editor**, **create** → **creator**, **investigate** → **investigator**. There is no meaningful difference between a word ending in -er and one in -or — both mean 'the person who does this.' The suffix is fixed for each word and cannot be changed.

**-ist** signals a practitioner of a field, skill, or ideology: **journal** → **journalist**, **art** → **artist**, **piano** → **pianist**, **novel** → **novelist**, **special** → **specialist**, **biology** → **biologist**, **economics** → **economist**, **chemistry** → **chemist**, **guitar** → **guitarist**. If you know the name of a field of study — biology, physics, chemistry, economics — the person who studies it is very likely to end in **-ist** (or its shortened form after dropping the field suffix: **psycholog-y → psychologist**).

A practical note: these three suffixes are never interchangeable for any specific word. There is no 'teacheror' or 'actist.' Each word has exactly one accepted form — and native speakers notice immediately when the wrong one appears. The most reliable approach: learn the most common person-nouns as fixed forms, and notice which suffix a new profession uses the first time you encounter it.

The most powerful use of everything you have learned in this material is what linguists call **morphological awareness** — using your knowledge of word parts to decode the meaning of words you have never seen before.

The process is simple. See an unknown word. Identify the suffix. That tells you the word class and the general meaning. Find the root. That tells you the specific meaning.

**Precarious** — ends in **-ous**, so it is an adjective meaning 'having the quality of' something. The root is Latin 'precari' (to pray, to beg for something from others) — suggesting something that depends on luck or other people's goodwill. Meaning: unstable, uncertain, likely to fail or fall. Even without knowing the Latin root, the suffix tells you it is an adjective describing a quality.

**Enforcement** — ends in **-ment**, so it is a noun for the result of an action. The root verb is 'enforce' (to make a rule be followed). Meaning: the act or system of making rules be followed. 'Law enforcement' — the system that enforces the law.

**Unforeseeable** — break it into parts: **un-** (not) + **fore-** (before) + **see** + **-able** (can be done). An event that could not be predicted or seen in advance. Four parts, all readable, one meaning derived entirely from the structure.

**Sustainability** — ends in **-ity** (a noun suffix related to **-ness**). The adjective is **sustainable**, which ends in **-able** (can be sustained). The root verb is **sustain** (to keep going without using everything up). 'Sustainability' is the quality of being sustainable.

This is the real payoff of learning word formation. You stop needing to look up every unknown word — you start reading through it. At B1-B2 level, this skill is one of the clearest markers of a confident reader in any language.

A few words in this family trap learners — either because the English meaning has drifted from what the suffix logic suggests, or because the word looks like a Portuguese cognate but behaves differently.

**Terrific** does not mean terrible. This is one of English's most counterintuitive words. The root is 'terror' — and **terrific** once did mean 'causing terror.' But the word shifted over centuries and now means wonderful, impressive, excellent. 'That's a terrific idea!' means it is a great idea. 'You did a terrific job' is a strong compliment. The family remains mixed: **terrifying** still means causing terror, **terrible** still means very bad — but **terrific** broke away and went in the opposite direction. Learn it as its own word, not as part of the terror-family logic.

**Sensible** is one of the most important false friends in this material. In English, **sensible** means reasonable, practical, showing good judgment. 'A sensible decision' is a wise one. 'She's a very sensible person' means she thinks clearly and avoids rash choices. The Portuguese 'sensível' — easily affected by emotions or stimuli — translates to **sensitive** in English, not **sensible**. These two words look nearly identical and mean completely different things. Mixing them up is one of the most common B1-level errors among Portuguese speakers.

**Comfortable** — a pronunciation trap rather than a meaning trap. In natural spoken English, this word typically has three syllables, not four: **COMF-ta-ble**. The second syllable disappears in connected speech. Many learners say 'com-FOR-ta-ble' (four syllables even in casual conversation), which sounds slightly deliberate to native ears. You will hear the compressed version in virtually every natural conversation — it is not careless speech, it is simply how the word sounds at normal speed.

**-tion words and Portuguese -ção words** — the overlap is enormous and genuinely useful: **information** / informação, **organization** / organização, **communication** / comunicação, **education** / educação, **production** / produção, **connection** / conexão. The pattern is almost perfectly reliable: if you know the Portuguese -ção noun, the English -tion noun exists and has the same meaning. The one trap is pronunciation: in English, -tion is always 'shun' (in-for-MAY-shun), not 'sowng' as in Portuguese. Reading the word and saying it correctly are two very different skills — and the pronunciation gap here is one of the most noticeable features of a non-native accent in English.
